title: 𒋳𒈠 𒀀𒉿𒈝
titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §66–78: The erased columns I — houses and neighbours (from the duplicate tablets)
part: Laws §66–78 · The erased columns I (Susa fragments and Assyrian copies)
draftNote: The § chips number the laws (Harper’s sectioning, still standard); long laws span several tap-units. Readings checked sign-by-sign against Harper’s 1904 edition.
source: Louvre stele, after R.F. Harper, The Code of Hammurabi, King of Babylon (Chicago, 1904): transliteration and autograph plates, List of Signs. Readings are Harper’s in modern subscript notation. Cuneiform in Old Babylonian monumental sign forms via the SantakkuM webfont by Sylvie Vanséveren (CC BY 4.0); pronunciation: conventional reconstructed Old Babylonian. Audio: a German synthetic voice reads the Akkadian word by word from these pronunciation rules (word stress after Huehnergard). It cannot hold a consonant long, so doubled consonants are heard single (šumma with one m), and the emphatics ṭ and q are heard as plain t and k. Fresh translations made directly from the Akkadian; Harper’s public-domain translation consulted for sense only.

images.caption: The stele in the Louvre: a single block of black basalt about 2.25 m tall. In the relief at the top, Hammurabi stands before the enthroned sun-god Šamaš, the god of justice; the laws run in columns of cuneiform below.
images.alt: The tall black basalt stele of Hammurabi in a museum gallery, a relief of the king and the god Šamaš at its top

about: The stele is erased here. After §65 the last seven columns of the front of the stone (XVII–XXIII, in Ungnad’s count) were chiselled smooth in antiquity, probably when the Elamite conquerors carried the stele away to Susa, and the laws that stood there reach us only from other ancient copies of the code, some of them broken: two Old Babylonian fragments found at Susa (Scheil’s Fragments I and II, here Susa-I and Susa-II) and two Assyrian copies from the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, written in Assyrian script more than a thousand years after Hammurabi (Rm. 277 and DT 81). Every unit below says which tablet its words come from, and what is lost is shown as a gap [ … ], never filled in. What survives is the house-and-neighbour block: the end of §66 (a man who gives his orchard to a merchant for a debt: the owner of the orchard takes the dates himself, pays the merchant the silver and its interest according to the tablet, and keeps the surplus dates), the first words of §67 (building a house), and, in Ungnad’s approximate numbering, only scraps of §70–74 (an owner of a house; one nearly whole law, §71, on buying a house that carries fief-duty), the broken §72, §73 and §74, the speech of §76 about a vacant plot, and §78 (a tenant sent away before his term). The numbers from 70 on are Ungnad’s approximate ones (“cca.”); §68–69, §75 and §77, and the stretches between these pieces, are not represented at all — nothing of them survives in the copies available. Kohler and Ungnad’s 1909 transliteration is the text; the signs follow it, checked against Ungnad’s autographs only where the small drawings were legible (the sign-by-sign check of every line was not completed, and the notes say where a doubt remains); the editors’ restorations in [ ] are not adopted as signs.

sentences.i: If a man has taken silver from a merchant, and his merchant presses him for it, and he has nothing to give, and he gives his orchard, once it has been put in order (?), to the merchant, and says to him, “Take away the dates, as many as are in the orchard, for your silver,” that merchant shall not agree. The owner of the orchard shall take the dates that are in the orchard, and he shall pay the merchant the silver and its interest according to his tablet, and the surplus dates …
sentences.n: From Scheil’s Fragment I from Susa (siglum Susa-I), column II: an Old Babylonian copy of the code found at Susa. The stele itself is erased here, so this law — §66, and that number is not approximate — is read from the duplicate tablet. What you need to read it: Kohler–Ungnad print an Akkadian word wherever the tablet has a logogram, and the signs here follow Ungnad’s autograph (1909). kaspam is KÙ.BABBAR as everywhere; tamkārim is DAM.GÀR with the ending -im written out; kirîm is {giš}KIRI₆, “orchard”; suluppî, “dates”, is written KA.LUM (Ungnad’s own reading, with a footnote — modern books read the same two signs ZÚ.LUM). ṣibat-zu is ṣibtum, “interest”, with -su written ZU (the stele writes the same word syllabically, ṣi-ba-zu, in §51; Ungnad prints this one as one Akkadian word, as he does his logograms, which fits MÁŠ): since Ungnad prints the word ṣibat before ZU, I took it for the logogram MÁŠ plus ZU, but I could not tell on the plate whether the tablet spells it with syllables instead. tarkibtim, rendered “the putting in order”, is a guess from the context (an orchard handed over after some work on it); the word has no parallel in the published parts, so the sense is uncertain. pî is the sign KA. isiršuma is from esērum, “to press, constrain”, a sense taken from the context (Ungnad’s own glossary entry for this verb is thin), so it is not certain. First occurrence of the pattern the whole code is built on: one long šumma-condition (a man takes silver, the merchant presses him, he has nothing to give, he hands over his orchard and says “take the dates”), and only then the ruling, tamkārum šū ul immagar, “that merchant shall not agree” (ul + present, a flat refusal). The offer is a quotation inside the condition: tabal is an imperative, “take away!”; ibbaššû is the N-stem of bašûm, “are to be found”, with the -u that closes a verb in a ša-clause; ša pî ṭuppišu is literally “that of the mouth of his tablet”, that is, as the tablet reads. Ungnad’s footnotes give variants for the Assyrian copy Rm. 277 (for the same words: šu, ag-ga-ra, pi-i, pi). The Susa signs are small and a few were hard to tell apart on the autograph; where I could not, the established reading is kept. The sentence goes on in the next unit.
sentences.ref: Susa-I col. II = stele col. XVII 2–24 (the old-Babylonian copy; Kohler–Ungnad p. 34)

sentences.i: … that are in the orchard — the owner of the orchard shall take (them).
sentences.n: From Rm. 277 (siglum Rm277), column II (Ungnad’s list of the Assyrian fragments gives XVII 9–32 as column II of this tablet): a copy of the code made in Assyrian script for the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh (Kuyunjik, seventh century BC). The Susa tablet is broken at this point and the stele itself is erased, so Kohler–Ungnad complete the end of §66 from this Assyrian copy and print it in italics. The first of the four lines (ša ina kirîm) is printed upright by Kohler–Ungnad, so it stands on the Susa tablet; only the last three are italic and so come from Rm. 277. The four lines return to words you have just read in the Susa lines: ša ina kirîm ibbaššû, bēl kirîm-ma ileqqi, “the surplus dates that are in the orchard — the owner of the orchard shall take them”. The last word is broken: Ungnad prints i-l[i-ki]; only the start of it stands on the tablet, so I wrote the sign I, the damaged sign LI and a gap, and [i-ki] — the editor’s restoration — is not adopted as signs. This is an Assyrian hand and I could not read its signs one by one; the signs follow Ungnad’s transliteration, and the Akkadian words printed there (kirîm) are written with the same logograms as in the Susa lines.
sentences.ref: Rm. 277 col. I = stele col. XVII 25–28 (Assyrian copy; the Susa tablet is broken here; Kohler–Ungnad p. 34, italic)

sentences.i: If a man builds (?) a house [and] the plot adjoining it (?) […] which […]
sentences.n: From Rm. 277 (siglum Rm277), column II (Ungnad’s list gives XVII 9–32 as column II of this tablet): the Assyrian copy of the code (Kuyunjik, Neo-Assyrian script). Only the opening of §67 survives — the Susa tablet is broken here and the stele is erased — and Kohler–Ungnad print it in italics. §67 is the first law of a new subject, buildings: šumma awīlum bītam ippēšma, “if a man builds a house and …”, the usual law shape (šumma, subject, present-tense verb; -ma joins the next clause). bītam is the logogram É (“house”), as in the earlier parts. tēḫûšu, “the plot adjoining it” (tēḫûm, Ungnad’s glossary: “adjoining piece, neighbouring plot — so apparently here”), is his guess and the sense is uncertain. Broken edges: Ungnad prints a-[wi-lum] and i-ip[-pi-eš-ma]; only a and i-ip are on the tablet, and the editor’s [wi-lum] and [-pi-eš-ma] are not adopted as signs, nor are the dotted gaps, which are shown as gaps. The rest of §67 and §68–69 are lost: Ungnad says only that column III of Fragment I, completed from column II of DT 81, is to be inserted here, and gives no text for the stretch between.
sentences.ref: Rm. 277 col. I = stele col. XVII 29–32 (only the opening of the law survives; Kohler–Ungnad p. 34, italic)

sentences.n: From Scheil’s Fragment I from Susa (siglum Susa-I), column III: an Old Babylonian copy of the code; the stele itself is erased here. Only the end of one line survives: one sign on the autograph, a diamond-shaped sign that I take for di, as Ungnad does, and the ending -šum, which he prints in italics, i.e. from DT 81 (the Assyrian copy that completes column III of Fragment I); the rest — [. . i-na], [iš] — is the editor’s restoration and is not adopted as signs. What the words give: i-na-di-iš-šum, inaddiššum, “he shall give him” (singular: inaddin + šum; “they will give him” would need inaddinūšum), from nadānum, “to give” — the end of a rule whose condition and subject are lost. The number 70 is Ungnad’s approximate number (“cca. 70”) for this scrap; the real position of the law is unknown.
sentences.ref: Susa-I col. III = stele col. XVIII 3 (only the end of one line: [. . i-na]-di-[iš]-šum 'they will give him'; Kohler–Ungnad p. 34, 'cca. 70')

sentences.i: If someone gives grain, silver or goods for a house that carries fief-duty, one belonging to his neighbour’s house, which he is buying, he forfeits whatever he gave, and the house returns to its owner. If that house carries no fief-duty, he may buy it, and for that house he shall give grain, silver or goods.
sentences.n: From Scheil’s Fragment I from Susa (siglum Susa-I), column III, completed from DT 81, column II: the Susa tablet is an Old Babylonian copy of the code, DT 81 an Assyrian copy (Kuyunjik, Neo-Assyrian script); the stele itself is erased here. Kohler–Ungnad print the Susa signs upright and the stretches taken from DT 81 in italics (marked ⟨ ⟩ in the established text); both are real signs of a real tablet, so I wrote all of them, and the ⟨ ⟩ stretches are the DT 81 ones. Where the page, as I read it, differs from the ⟨ ⟩ marks (line 12: only -am is italic; line 13: -tim and a-ti), I could not settle it on the autograph. [be-li] and [in] are the editor’s restorations and are not adopted as signs: the first is shown as a gap. The number 71 is Ungnad’s approximate number (“cca. 71”). How to read it: bīt ilkim, “house of the fief-duty” (ilkum, met in §26–41), is a house that carries service to the crown — it may not be bought, as the fief-land of §36–41 may not. še’am kaspam u bīšam, “grain, silver and goods”, is the code’s stock list of payments, again with še’am as ŠE-am (the complement -am) and kaspam as KÙ.BABBAR. inaddin is the present of nadānum, “he gives”; ītelli, “he forfeits”, the perfect of elûm “to go up”: what he gave has gone up out of his hands. bītum ana bēlīšu itâr, “the house returns to its owner”, uses itâr as in §26–41. The law runs in two halves, joined by šumma again: the house with fief-duty (the buyer loses what he paid) and the house without (he may buy, išām, and pay). ša bīt itêšu, “which (is) of the house of his neighbour”, is my reading of a hard phrase: I take i-te-šu for itêšu (“his neighbour”); the sense is uncertain. The same goes for ša išammu: I took it as “which he buys”, but it could as well be the subject, “he who buys”.
sentences.ref: Susa-I col. III, completed from DT 81 col. II = stele col. XVIII 4–17 (⟨ ⟩ = DT 81; Kohler–Ungnad p. 35, 'cca. 71')

sentences.n: From Scheil’s Fragment I from Susa (siglum Susa-I), column III: an Old Babylonian copy of the code, broken at the right-hand edge; the stele itself is erased here. What is left are line-beginnings, and Kohler–Ungnad’s right-hand restorations — ba-lum i-[te-šu(?)] i-te-[pu-uš](?), i-na bît [ra-ma-ni-šu(?)], i-te-[ip-pu-uš], a-na [bît i-te-šu](?) — are the editor’s conjectures with his own question marks: they are not adopted as signs and the broken ends are shown as gaps. Only the signs visible on the autograph are written: šum-ma a-wi, ni, ba-lum i, i-te, i-na É, i-te, a-na. The number 72 is Ungnad’s approximate number (“cca. 72”). What can be read: balum is “without”, ina bīt “in the house of …”, itepuš / iteppuš forms of epēšum, “to do, to build”, and ana “to / for” — the law seems to concern building in or against a neighbour’s house, but nothing can be said beyond that; the English below gives only what the signs give.

sentences.n: From Rm. 277 (siglum Rm277), column III: the Assyrian copy of the code (Kuyunjik, Neo-Assyrian script), printed in italics by Kohler–Ungnad; the stele is erased here and no older copy is left for this law. Only the beginnings of six lines survive — a few signs each: na…, bēl [bītim], šumma bi…, bēl [bītim], mimma [ša …], iri[ab]. The restorations in [ ] (bîtim, ša, i-a-ab) are the editor’s and are not adopted as signs; the broken ends are shown as gaps. In the last line only the start of the second sign (ri) is on the tablet, but the word is clearly iriab, “he shall replace” (riābum, as in §8 and §53). The number 73 is Ungnad’s approximate number (“cca. 73”). From the pieces: a house-owner (bēl bītim) is the subject, and the law ends with the usual penalty, “whatever [ … ] he shall replace”; bi… is perhaps the start of bītum, “house” (Ungnad’s own doubtful footnote).

From your vacant plot they will breach […] the house (?) to you […] he set […] in the crossing-over […] to you […] [silver (?)]”
sentences.n: From Scheil’s Fragment II from Susa (siglum Susa-II), column I: an Old Babylonian copy of the code; the stele itself is erased here. Ungnad’s number is “cca. 76” — an approximate number, not the law’s real place. This is direct speech and the sense is unclear even to Kohler–Ungnad, who translate it as a guess: it concerns a quarrel about a vacant plot (nidītum, the word met in §61 for a plot left lying) and a part of the building that has been “crossed over” (nabalkattum, from the root of “to cross over”; šubalkutum is its causative). The words that can be read: dannin is a D-stem imperative of danānum, “make firm”; ištu bītika, “from your house”; ana bēl niditim, “to the owner of the vacant plot”; niditka epuš, “make (use of) your vacant plot”; ipallašūnim, “they will breach”, palāšum as in the house-breaking laws. Sign doubts: Ungnad’s own question marks on at (line 2), da (3), iš (4), uš (5), the doubtful bi (line 9) and -am (line 14) are his and remain doubts. [ ] marks the editor’s restorations and the broken stretches: they are not adopted as signs and are shown as gaps; where only part of a sign is lost — [n]i, e[l], [iš-t]u — I wrote the sign as visible. The plate agrees with the line count, and the sign counts of the preserved rows are close to Ungnad’s, but the small Susa signs were not all legible to me, so his readings are kept.
sentences.ref: Susa-II col. I = stele col. XVIII 50–63 (Scheil's Fragment II; Kohler–Ungnad p. 35–36, 'cca. 76'; speech: '… you have crossed over … from your house … to the owner of the field')

sentences.i: A man who is a tenant has given the owner of the house his whole rent for the year, and the owner of the house has told the tenant to go out before his days are full: the owner of the house, because he made the tenant leave his house before his days were full, [forfeits] the silver that the tenant gave him. (The opening “if” of the law is lost.)
sentences.n: From DT 81 (siglum DT81), column III: an Assyrian copy of the code (Kuyunjik, library of Ashurbanipal, Neo-Assyrian script). The stele is erased here and the Old Babylonian copy is lost at this place, so Kohler–Ungnad’s whole text of this law is the Assyrian copy, printed entirely in italics; I wrote its signs as real signs of that tablet. Ungnad warns that the restorations are in part doubtful, and every [ ] is the editor’s restoration, not adopted as signs: the broken ends and whole broken lines are shown as gaps, and the opening “if” of the law is lost. The number 78 is Ungnad’s approximate number (“cca. 78”). Where only the end of a sign is lost — wa-ṣ[a-am], a[š-šum], aš-bu-u[m] — the sign is written as visible. Reading help: kasap kiṣrišu is KÙ.BABBAR (construct kasap, “the silver of”) plus kiṣri, written KA.SAR (Ungnad’s footnote), “his rent” — a tenant’s payment for the year (ša šanat, “of the year”); wāšbum “the dweller”, the tenant; lā malûtim, “not full”, malûm “to be full”: the days of the lease unfinished; waṣâm iqtabi is “he said (that he should) go out”; ušeṣû is the Š-stem of waṣûm, “he made go out”; ītelli “he forfeits”, as in the house-with-fief law above. The last word of the law, [ītelli], is wholly lost: it is the editor’s restoration from §71, shown as a gap, and bracketed in the English. Ungnad’s footnote on aš-bu-u[m] says that reading is “probably right” after Peiser, so it is the least certain word of the law. At the word u-[še-ṣu-u] the page prints the sign as zu (ú-[še-zu-ú]), the pinned text as ṣu: only the first sign u is written. In line 8 the pinned text shows -šu complete, but Ungnad’s page brackets it (ûmi^mi[-šú]): I follow the page. This is a typical law of rent: a tenant who has paid the year’s rent in full may not be put out early; if the landlord does it, he loses the rent.
sentences.ref: DT 81 col. III = stele col. XIX 25–42 (Assyrian copy, entirely restored in italics by Kohler–Ungnad p. 36, 'cca. 78' — the Old Babylonian copy is lost here; he cautions that the restorations are partly doubtful)

glossary.awīlum: man; the free citizen, the code’s first legal class
glossary.balum: without · (ina) balum bēl eqlim “without (the consent of) the owner of the field”
glossary.bašûm: to exist, arise: ibbaššû “which arose” · lā ibaššišum “there is not to him” (= he has none), with dative -šum
glossary.bašûm-N: N-stem of bašûm: to be there, be found: ibbaššû (present, 3rd plural, in a ša-clause) “which are found”
glossary.bēlum: owner, lord: bēl ḫulqim “owner of the lost property” · owner of a field, bēl eqlim; bēl ḫubullim “creditor” · bēl kirîm “owner of the orchard”
glossary.bīšum: movable property, goods, possessions: bīšašu “his goods”
glossary.danānum-D: D-stem of danānum “to be strong”: to strengthen, make firm (a dike): dunnunim (infinitive) “to strengthen”, udanninma (preterite, with -ma) “he strengthened, and …”
glossary.elûm: to go up; here: to forfeit: ina kaspišu ītelli “he goes up out of his silver” — his money is gone · to come up: īteliānim (perfect, feminine plural, with the ventive -nim) “(the sheep) have come up”
glossary.epēšum: to do, make: epēšim “doing” · to work (land): ippeš(ma) (present): eqlam šipram ippeš “he shall do the work on the field” · to build (?) (a house): bītam ippēšma(?) “he builds a house, and”, the verb broken; iteppuš (?) in a broken line
glossary.esērum: UNCERTAIN: to press, constrain (a debtor): isiršuma “he pressed him, and” (preterite + -šu + -ma); the sense is taken from context
glossary.gamārum: to bring to completion; D-stem gummurum — mugammer “who heaps up (to the full)” · to finish: lā igmur(ma) (preterite) “he did not finish”
glossary.ilkum: the fief-duty — service owed to the crown for land held: ilikšu illak “he shall perform his duty”; the keyword of §§26–41
glossary.ina: in, from · at (ina ebūrim “at harvest”); out of (ina bilat kirîm “out of the orchard’s yield”)
glossary.itûm: neighbour, the adjoining one: kīma itêšu “like its neighbour” (the neighbouring field)
glossary.ištu: after, since; from; as a conjunction, “after, once”: ištu … īteliānim “after … have come up”
glossary.išûm: to have: lā īšu “he has not”
glossary.kaspum: silver — the code’s money, written KÙ.BABBAR “shining precious-metal” · kaspim: mišil mana kaspim “half a mina of silver”
glossary.kirûm: orchard, garden (written {giš}SAR, the KIRI₆ sign): kirāšu “his orchard”
glossary.kiṣrum: UNCERTAIN: rent, a tenant’s payment for a house (written KA.SAR, per Ungnad’s footnote): kasap kiṣri(šu) “the silver of (his) rent”; the sense is taken from context
glossary.magārum: to agree, consent: imtagarma (perfect, with -ma) “has come to an agreement”, said of a settlement made with another party (itti …)
glossary.mala: as many as, as much as (introducing a relative clause): mala ina kirîm ibbaššû “as many as are in the orchard”
glossary.malûm: to be full; malûtim (feminine plural adjective, genitive) “full”: lā malûtim “not full”, said of the days of a lease; malû… is a broken form
glossary.nabalkattum: UNCERTAIN: apparently “crossing-over”, a noun from the root BLKT of nabalkutum “to cross over”; nabalkatka “your crossing-over (?)”; the sense is a guess, and the word is broken in places (naba…, …katim)
glossary.nadānum: to give, pay: inaddin, iddinam, iddinušum; nadānim “to give” · iddin “he gave”; ana kaspim nadānum “to sell”: inaddinūma (present, plural) “they shall sell, and …”
glossary.nidītum: land left lying, an unplanted patch, part left over (from nadûm “to leave”): nidītam (accusative)
glossary.palāšum: to break through, breach (a house wall): iplūš “he broke in”
glossary.pûm: mouth (the KA sign); ina pī mātim “in the mouth of the land” · ana pî ṣimdat šarrim “according to the mouth of the king’s ordinance”
glossary.qabûm: to speak, say: iqbû, iqtabi, iqabbûma
glossary.suluppû: dates, the date crop (a collective noun, treated as plural; two signs, read ZÚ.LUM today, KA.LUM in Ungnad’s reading): suluppî (oblique case); suluppî watrūtim “the surplus dates”
glossary.tabālum: to take away, carry off: itabbal · tabal “take!” (imperative)
glossary.tamkārum: merchant (written tam-KAR §32, DAM.GÀR §40): the ransom-fronting, land-buying businessman of the code
glossary.tarkibtum: UNCERTAIN: perhaps the putting in order of an orchard handed over (a noun, perhaps from rakābum “to mount”): ištu tarkibtim “after the putting in order (?)” (genitive); the sense is a guess from context
glossary.târum: to return: ul itârma “he shall never again …”
glossary.tēḫûm: UNCERTAIN: perhaps “adjoining piece, neighbouring plot” (Ungnad’s guess, his glossary hedged); tēḫûšu “the plot adjoining it (?)”
glossary.watārum: to exceed; Š-stem — mušāter “who makes surpassing”; ušāterūšu “they made it supreme” · watrum “surplus, in excess”: watrūtim (feminine plural) said of the surplus dates
glossary.wašābum: to sit: ul uššab “he shall not sit” (the stone writes uš-ta-ab — a carver’s slip Harper flags) · to dwell: wāšbum (participle, contracted) “the dweller, the tenant” (a conjectured reading, aš-bu-u[m]); wa… “dwell-” in broken forms
glossary.waṣûm: to go out; ūṣiamma “he came forward”
glossary.waṣûm-Š: Š-stem of waṣûm “to go out”: to send out, bring out; of land, to take on lease: ana irrišūtim ušēṣi “he took (a field) for cultivation”
glossary.šakānum: to set, place: išakkanūšumma “they shall set for him (a term), and” · išakkanūšum (present, plural, dative -šum) “they shall place (it) for him”, i.e. count it to him
glossary.šattum: year: šattam (syllabic, §31) or MU (the year-sign, §30) · šattim (genitive); plural šanātim “years” (ša šanātim “of the years”); MU 4{kam}, said erbe šanātim “four years”
glossary.šubalkutum: UNCERTAIN: Š-stem of the root BLKT (nabalkutum “to cross over”): “to make cross over”; ušbalakatūnim (present, 3rd plural, with ventive -nim) “they make (it) cross over (?)”; the sense is a guess
glossary.šumma: if — the word that opens every law of the code
glossary.šuāti: that, the aforesaid · as the independent pronoun “him”: šuāti u bīšašu “him and his goods”
glossary.šâmum: to buy: ištām “he bought”, išammu “he buys”
glossary.ūmum: day; ūmišu “daily” (written UD-mi-šu) · plural “days”: ūmī (written UD-mi-) “days”: ina ūmīšu lā malûtim “in his days not full” (the days of a lease)
glossary.ṭuppum: the clay tablet; the deed: ṭuppašu iḫḫeppi “his tablet shall be smashed” — the sale annulled physically
